summary:
Ucayali stands under the national framework of Peru. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. Any trans visitor to Ucayali is subject to these national rules rather than to a regional regime of its own.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved, and exempted from a second vote, the bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. The exceptions are narrow: custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The provision binds public facilities throughout Ucayali.

The legislative route to that ban ran through the Women and Family Commission, which on 20 February 2025 unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. The same committee draft barred trans people from restrooms not matching their birth sex, set the exceptions listed above, and prohibited 'ambiguous' bathroom signage.

LGBTI activist Gianna Camacho warned at that stage that restroom access would be left to the personal judgment of security staff, including whether to demand identity checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Her warning bears on how the rule is applied at a door in Ucayali, where a guard's discretion rather than a document decides entry.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP separately found the provision implicitly frames trans and non-binary people as harassment risks and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity' alongside other 'ambiguous' restroom wording. Its vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. These speech and signage restrictions apply to Ucayali's hotels, restaurants, shops and municipal buildings.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, so a visitor assaulted in Ucayali on grounds of gender identity has no hate-crime provision to invoke.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. The Inter-American Court had held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings, including clinics in Ucayali. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's position on LGBT hate-crime coverage is unusual in its subregion: only Paraguay and Guyana share the absence of such provisions, so the low level of legal protection is a national condition rather than an isolated local gap.

The recorded toll understates the risk. The 2024 report's co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, described the published figures as a sub-registry, meaning incidents that never enter official statistics; the 54 killings recorded between 2020 and 2023 are therefore a floor, not an estimate.

The origin of the restroom restriction shows how far the regime is intended to reach. A July 2023 social-media complaint about labels at Jorge Chávez airport, a transport hub serving travellers, produced bills that now govern ordinary public facilities, which places trans visitors in Ucayali under a rule shaped by a traveller-facing setting.

The pace of remedy is slow. Azul Rojas Marín's case took close to two decades and multiple stages, including the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, before three officers were sentenced in December 2025, so prospective protection and actual redress operate on very different timelines.

Regional jurisprudence points the other way from Peruvian legislation: Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights treats gender identity as protected personal autonomy and obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights, and IDEHPUCP's analysis measures the 2025 law against the Peruvian Constitution and the American Convention on Human Rights.
localsOnly:
Article 5 of the April 2025 law governs residents' daily access to public sanitary services, and the same package determines what signage a business, school or municipal office in Ucayali may display; 'women in their diversity' and other inclusive wording is prohibited.

Because the 2017 repeal removed LGBT provisions from the Penal Code's hate-crime articles, residents have no hate-crime mechanism to invoke for identity-motivated assault, and complaints can end as they did at a gym, where a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination claim.

Health care moved in a protective direction: in June 2024 the national health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, which applies to facilities treating residents of Ucayali.

The April 2025 law's child-protection articles also constrain residents' access to media and educational material: article 4 reaches advertising and media content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rose from three to four years.

Constitutional challenge remains available. Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights are the grounds IDEHPUCP relies on against the restroom ban, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist legal challenge.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Ucayali-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. Nothing in it records a restroom exclusion, a police incident, a court case or a local regulation originating in Ucayali, so the region's profile rests entirely on how the national framework binds it.

Not sourced: whether regional or municipal authorities in Ucayali have issued implementing instructions for article 5, and which facilities treat it as binding. The inventory records the national law's approval on 2 April 2025 and the February 2025 committee stage, not local application.

Unresolved: how the article 5 exceptions for custody, medical need, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities are applied in practice by security staff in Ucayali, and whether identity checks demanded at restroom doors generate complaints that any body records.

Not sourced: Ucayali-specific figures on violence against trans people, and whether the 2024 report's national totals include cases from the region. The sub-registry caveat raised by Gianna Camacho applies to the national data with no regional breakdown available.

Unresolved: the final promulgation mechanics of the April 2025 package after the Plenary's 2 April 2025 approval and exemption from second vote, and whether any subsequent constitutional challenge has reached the articles on signage or media content.
